items.title_original: You've got the grades, but don't pass on your health
items.summary_original: Medicines and medical devices regulator issues health advice for teens off to university.

items.article_text_original: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) congratulates everyone celebrating their A level results today (13 August). With the prospect of heading to university a few short weeks away, now is the time for young people to check they are up to date with their vaccinations and have the medicines and medical devices they need to stay well as they hit freshers’ week. These tips will stand you in good stead even if you’re taking another route following your results. Phil Tregunno, MHRA Deputy Director of Patient Safety Monitoring, said: “Securing your place at uni is an exciting milestone. It may be your first time living away from home and taking charge of your own health and wellbeing. Get prepared now, so when you arrive, you can focus on settling in and enjoying university life.” Meningitis B Meningitis B is a serious infection which can have long-term impact on your health and is potentially life-threatening. It can be contagious, so students living in university halls or shared accommodation and socialising together can be particularly at risk. The best protection against contracting Meningitis B is to get the Men B vaccine. The MenB vaccination is being delivered in slightly different ways across the UK. Find out more about whether you are eligible for the MenB vaccine, and how you can get it here: Meningococcal B (MenB) time limited vaccination offer - GOV.UK. It requires two doses, so time is of the essence before you head off to university. Patient safety is the MHRA’s number one priority. We approve, test and monitor all vaccines used in the UK, so you can be confident that they are safe and effective. Even after we’ve approved a vaccine for use, we test every single batch to make sure each one meets our high safety standards. We remain alert to any potential safety concerns and our most important partner in that safety monitoring is you. You can use the MHRA Yellow Card reporting scheme to report any suspected side effects from a vaccine. For more information about meningitis, read our patient factsheet. We have also published a vaccine safety patient factsheet to give patients and the public clear, accessible and evidence-based information about how vaccines work and how their safety is assured. Asthma The autumn term heralds the start of the coughs and colds season which can be particularly difficult for people with asthma. Check your asthma inhalers are in date and take them as prescribed. If you have a preventer inhaler take this every day, and use your reliever inhaler when you have symptoms of asthma. This should always be carried with you. If your inhaler does not have a dose counter or dose indicator, to avoid using an empty inhaler and to know when to order a new one, it is important to keep a tally of doses and compare that with the number of doses on the labelling of the inhaler – inhalers may still have residual liquid in them even when all the medicine doses have been used, but won’t be effective. If you use a spacer, make sure you have this too. If you experience symptoms and your inhaler is not helping, then seek urgent medical help. Helpful information which is still up to date can be found on the NHS England – London’s #AskAboutAsthma campaign website. Adrenaline auto-injectors Adrenaline auto-injectors (AAIs) are an important healthcare product used for those at risk of anaphylaxis and can save lives. If you have one or more allergies you may have been prescribed an AAI product such as Epipen or Jext. Anaphylaxis can be fatal. Remember the following: - There are three different types of AAIs – make sure you know how to use yours. - Always follow the instructions. - Always carry two in-date AAIs with you. - Check the expiry dates regularly and replace them before they expire. More information about these products, including a video on our AAI safety campaign, can be found here. Colds, flu and antibiotics Colds and flu are caused by viruses, not bacteria. Antibiotics won’t help so don’t take them. Ask your local pharmacy for advice on alleviating symptoms. If you are prescribed antibiotics, take the full course as directed by your GP, nurse or pharmacist. Taking antibiotics when not needed and not finishing the course is a major driver of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) development. Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) is a global issue which claimed over a million lives in 20211 across the world. AMR is where bacteria and other microorganisms have adapted to survive the antibiotics we use to fight them, and this problem is made worse when antibiotics are used when they are not needed. If you do not take a course of antibiotics that have been prescribed for you, dispose of them by taking them to your local pharmacy – do not throw them down the sink or the toilet, or put them in the bin. You can also read more about the MHRA’s work in tackling AMR here.

items.title_original: MHRA reaffirms the safety of childhood vaccination
items.summary_original: Vaccination is one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against many serious infectious diseases
items.summary_ai_original: Vaccination is one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against many serious infectious diseases Dr Alison Cave, Chief Safety Officer at the MHRA, said: “Multiple large, well-conducted studies involving millions of children worldwide have consistently demonstrated that there is no evidence that vaccines cau
items.article_text_original: Vaccination is one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against many serious infectious diseases Dr Alison Cave, Chief Safety Officer at the MHRA, said: “Multiple large, well-conducted studies involving millions of children worldwide have consistently demonstrated that there is no evidence that vaccines cause autism in children. “Vaccination remains one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against serious and potentially life-threatening diseases, supported by decades of scientific evidence in the UK and internationally. “The benefits of vaccination are endorsed by the NHS and all major UK public health and paediatric bodies as part of the recommended routine childhood vaccination schedule. “All vaccines approved for use in the UK undergo a rigorous assessment of their safety, quality and efficacy and once approved for use, we continuously monitor their safety through robust surveillance systems, real-world data, and international evidence. “We encourage parents to follow NHS guidance on vaccination and speak to a healthcare professional if they have any questions. “Patient safety is our top priority. We encourage anyone to report any suspected side effects to us via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.” Notes to Editors: - Childhood vaccination is recommended by the NHS, the World Health Organization, and public health authorities globally as the most effective way to protect children from serious infectious diseases. - Before approval, all vaccines undergo robust independent assessment by the MHRA to ensure they meet strict standards of safety, quality, and efficacy. - The UK childhood vaccination schedule is informed by evidence-based recommendations from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) and supported by NHS clinical guidance. - Multiple large, well-conducted international studies, including national registry studies and sibling-controlled studies, have found no evidence that vaccines cause autism in children. - In 2.56 million US children, researchers found no association between MMR vaccination before age 2 and childhood autism. (Burstain, et al, Vaccine Reports (2026) - A major meta-analysis of data from over 1.26 million children in cohort studies and nearly 10,000 children in case-control studies found no association between vaccination and autism and autism spectrum disorder (Taylor, et al., Vaccine (2014) - Some vaccines contain substances called adjuvants that boost the body’s immune response to the vaccine. A commonly used vaccine adjuvant is aluminium, although this isn’t used in the MMR vaccine. A recent large-scale study did not find evidence to support an increased risk for neurodevelopmental disorders including autism, with early childhood exposure to aluminium containing vaccines. - The MHRA has published a vaccine safety patient factsheet to give patients and the public clear, accessible and evidence-based information about how vaccines work and how their safety is assured and a meningitis patient factsheet to help people understand meningitis, recognise its potentially urgent symptoms, and understand the role and safety of vaccination to help prevent it. - The MHRA conducts continuous safety surveillance through the Yellow Card scheme, analysis of large healthcare datasets, review of international safety data, and there is ongoing review by independent scientific experts. - Should new evidence indicate a change in vaccine safety, the MHRA will act promptly to update guidance and information for healthcare professionals and the public. - Parents and carers should continue to follow NHS vaccination guidance to protect children from preventable diseases such as measles, meningitis, and whooping cough. - Members of the public and healthcare professionals are encouraged to report any suspected side effect from medicines and vaccines through the MHRA’s Yellow Card scheme. - The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that benefits justify any risks. - The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care. - For media enquiries, please contact newscentre@mhra.gov.uk or call 020 3080 7651.

Washington, D.C., 8 August 2026 (PAHO) – In a new Epidemiological Alert, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) called on countries across the Americas to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and rapid outbreak response measures amid rising measles cases across the Region. The call comes as measles transmission remains active in several countries and the Americas records its highest number of confirmed cases in more than two decades. As of epidemiological week 28 of 2026, ending on 18 July, countries and territories in the Americas had reported 47,459 confirmed measles cases. A total of 44 deaths have been reported in three countries. The number of cases is more than three times higher than the total reported during all of 2025, when 15,011 confirmed cases and 32 deaths were documented. Guatemala, Mexico, the United States and Peru account for 95% of confirmed cases reported so far this year. Although some of the Region's largest outbreaks have recently shown signs of slowing, transmission remains active in several countries. A public health risk assessment published this week by PAHO continues to classify the public health risk associated with measles in the Americas as very high. This classification is based on ongoing outbreaks, suboptimal vaccination coverage, the accumulation of susceptible individuals, and increased mobility linked to international travel and mass gatherings, factors that facilitate the importation and spread of the virus within and between countries. The assessment also highlights the increase in measles-related deaths reported in 2026 compared with 2025, the detection of cases in new geographic areas, and the disproportionate impact of outbreaks on populations facing barriers to healthcare, including Indigenous communities and groups with low vaccination coverage. "Measles leaves no room for complacency. We know how to stop it: achieving high vaccination coverage, detecting suspected cases early, and responding rapidly to interrupt chains of transmission," said Daniel Salas, Executive Manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. "Every outbreak exposes immunity gaps that must be urgently addressed, particularly among children, under-vaccinated communities, and populations with limited access to health services." Measles is one of the world's most contagious diseases. It spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The disease can cause fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and rash, and may lead to serious complications including pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness and death. Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent infection and stop transmission. According to PAHO's epidemiological alert, Guatemala has reported 30,371 confirmed cases and 26 deaths, the largest number of cases reported in the Region this year. It is followed by Mexico with 12,255 cases and 17 deaths, the United States with 2,260 cases, Peru with 1,277 cases, and Canada with 1,107 cases. The number of confirmed cases reported in 2026 is the highest recorded in the Americas since 2004, the highest level observed in the Region in the past 22 years. The regional situation reflects a broader global resurgence of the disease. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data, 186,168 measles cases had been reported worldwide by July 2026, representing a 12% increase compared with the same period in 2025. PAHO warned that young children not yet eligible for their first vaccine dose, unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals, Indigenous communities, migrants, displaced populations, and other groups facing barriers to healthcare remain at increased risk of severe disease and death. The Organization reiterated that achieving and maintaining at least 95% coverage with two doses of measles-containing vaccine is essential to interrupt transmission, protect vulnerable populations, and support efforts to restore the Region's measles elimination status. PAHO continues to provide technical cooperation to countries to strengthen surveillance, accelerate vaccination efforts, improve outbreak preparedness and response, and reinforce risk communication, particularly in areas with ongoing transmission and significant immunity gaps.
